tier_reason: Upgraded from C to A. The benchmark code is public: json/json_test.go has a TestMain -package switch plus BenchmarkMarshal/BenchmarkUnmarshal, and the Makefile bench-simple target on the `benchmarks` branch (the branch PR #77 says the README numbers were re-run from) gives the exact go test flags; its -count 5 matches the n=5+5 in the tables. The README names the CPU (Core i9-8950HK) and pins the baseline as 'encoding/json (v1.16.2)'. That label can only mean the Go 1.16.2 toolchain, because both implementations are compiled into one test binary.

corrections.claimed_speedup: Vs encoding/json v1.16.2 (Go 1.16.2 stdlib), Core i9-8950HK, benchstat n=5+5: Marshal/*json.codeResponse2 6.40ms -> 3.82ms (-40.29%), Unmarshal 28.1ms -> 5.6ms (-80.21%); speed 303 -> 507 MB/s (+67.47%) marshal and 69.2 -> 349.6 MB/s (+405.42%) unmarshal (~1.68x marshal, ~5.0x unmarshal, derived from page data); Unmarshal alloc 1.80MB -> 0.02MB (-99.14%) and 76.6k -> 0.1k allocs/op (-99.92%). Vs json-iterator/go v1.1.10: Marshal 6.19ms -> 3.82ms (-38.26%; 313 -> 507 MB/s, +61.91%, ~1.62x derived from page data), Unmarshal 8.52ms -> 5.55ms (-34.84%; 228 -> 350 MB/s, +53.50%, ~1.54x derived from page data).
corrections.compiler_and_flags: Go 1.16.2 (the page pins the baseline as encoding/json v1.16.2, which is the Go 1.16.2 stdlib; both implementations are built into one `go test` binary and selected with the harness's -package flag); default gc build flags; run as `go test -v -run '^$' -bench '(Marshal|Unmarshal)$/codeResponse' -benchmem -cpu 1 -count 5 ./json [-package encoding/json | -package github.com/json-iterator/go]` (Makefile target bench-simple on the `benchmarks` branch, per PR #77), compared with benchstat
corrections.workload: Marshal (Append into a reused buffer) and Unmarshal of the Go stdlib's encoding/json testdata/code.json.gz corpus, loaded into the repo's codeResponse2 struct (json/json_test.go BenchmarkMarshal/BenchmarkUnmarshal, `(Marshal|Unmarshal)$/codeResponse` subtests), single CPU (-cpu 1), 5 runs per side, compared with benchstat against encoding/json (Go 1.16.2) and json-iterator/go v1.1.10. The numbers were re-run by hand from the `benchmarks` branch in March 2021 (PR #77). The current CI does not produce them: it only benchmarks master against the PR head.
corrections.caveats: First-party numbers from March 2021 (Go 1.16.2, i9-8950HK laptop CPU, PR #77) that have not been refreshed. Both the stdlib and this library have changed since, and the repo now declares go 1.23. The README says the CI compares against the stdlib, but the current .github/workflows/benchmark.yml only compares master with the PR head (ubuntu-latest, Go 1.24). Only one corpus is shown (code.json.gz into codeResponse2). In the harness, segmentio's Unmarshal calls Parse(..., ZeroCopy), so strings alias the input buffer, while the stdlib side calls json.Unmarshal, which copies; zero-copy mode accounts for part of the Unmarshal time and allocation gap. Error messages differ from encoding/json.

notes: The A tier depends on reading 'encoding/json (v1.16.2)' as the Go 1.16.2 toolchain. If a literal 'Go X.Y' statement is required, this entry falls back to C. I fixed the json-iterator marshal ratio from ~1.53x to ~1.62x. I also corrected last_commit to the master head, 2026-03-10; the repo's pushed_at of 2026-06-25 comes from the non-default branch cstj/migrate-runs-on-twilio-runners.

tier_reason: The README tables compare directly against encoding/json using public benchmark code (benchmarks/benchmarks_test.go: benchmarkEncodingJson, benchmarkJsoniter, benchmarkSimdJson). However, no CPU model, Go version or build flags are stated; the only environment detail is the -32 GOMAXPROCS suffix. That is first-party with partial methodology, so C.

corrections.claimed_speedup: README: 'Compared to Golang's standard package encoding/json, simdjson-go is about 10x faster' and it 'runs on average at about 40% to 60% of the speed of simdjson'. The per-file benchcmp table (default settings, i.e. string copying on) ranges from 2.34x (Numbers, 70.42 -> 165.04 MB/s) to 16.50x (Gsoc_2018, 160.17 -> 2642.88 MB/s), e.g. Twitter 95.17 -> 1072.59 MB/s (11.27x) and Citm_catalog 101.29 -> 1270.02 MB/s (12.54x). The 14 per-file speedups have an arithmetic mean of ~7.5x and a geometric mean of ~6.4x (derived from page data), so the '10x' headline is above the README's own table. Vs json-iterator/go the table shows 3.19x-12.38x per file.
corrections.workload: encoding/json.Unmarshal and json-iterator (ConfigCompatibleWithStandardLibrary) Unmarshal into interface{}, versus simdjson-go's simdjson.Parse building its internal tape (no Go values materialized), on 14 test files (apache_builds, canada, citm_catalog, github_events, gsoc_2018, instruments, marine_ik, mesh, mesh_pretty, numbers, random, twitter, twitterescaped, update_center). Results are go test -bench output compared with benchcmp, with GOMAXPROCS=32 per the -32 benchmark suffix. Code: benchmarks/benchmarks_test.go.
corrections.caveats: The comparison is not like-for-like: simdjson-go only parses into its tape, while encoding/json and json-iterator build full interface{} trees. The README itself says simdjson 'provides different output than traditional unmarshal functions'. No CPU model or Go version is stated, only GOMAXPROCS=32. The README numbers match the WithCopyStrings(true) 'copy' rows, but the current benchmarks/benchmarks_test.go runs simdjson with WithCopyStrings(false). Issue #35 (2021) reported that the earlier published numbers could not be reproduced at HEAD. That led to the current table (PR #36, May 2021), which has not been refreshed since. amd64 only, with AVX2+CLMUL required and no fallback. The last commit was 2025-08-26 (~13 months ago), so the entry is stale by this pipeline's rule.

notes: The record is accurate: the numbers belong to the encoding/json benchcmp table, and license, stars (2,044) and the stale status all check out. I added the apples-to-oranges caveat (tape parse vs full unmarshal) and a derived mean showing the README's '10x' headline is generous. I did not verify 'used by MinIO' beyond MinIO owning the repo, so I left it unchanged.

tier_reason: The README compares ssrJSON directly with stdlib json, both as text ranges and as ratio labels in the v0.0.17 charts, and links public benchmark code (Nambers/ssrJSON-benchmark, src/ssrjson_benchmark/benchmark.py). The README charts name no CPU, though. No Clang version or build flags are stated for the measured build; the per-CPU PDF reports cover other versions and record only the CPython build compiler. First-party with partial methodology, so C.

corrections.claimed_speedup: README text: 'ssrjson.dumps() is about 4x-31x as fast as json.dumps()' and 'ssrjson.loads() is about 2x-8x as fast as json.loads()' for both str and bytes input (Python3.14, x86-64, AVX2). TL;DR: 'faster than or nearly as fast as orjson ... on most benchmark cases'. The page's v0.0.17 charts label these ratios vs json. dumps to str: canada 23.07x, mesh 17.79x, github 9.63x, twitter 7.52x, simple_object_zh 4.93x. loads str: canada 7.75x, mesh 4.49x, github 3.40x, simple_object_zh 2.58x, twitter 2.54x. dumps_to_bytes: canada 26.27x. orjson on the same charts: twitter loads str 1.80x, canada dumps to str 16.67x.
corrections.hardware: Not stated for the README's v0.0.17 dumps/loads charts, which say only 'x86-64, AVX2'. The float-formatting micro-benchmark names Apple M1 and AMD R7-7840H. The linked ssrJSON-benchmark repo publishes per-CPU PDF reports (e.g. i7-13700K AVX2 for 0.0.21 with Python 3.14.6 built by GCC 15.3.0; also i7-11370H, Ryzen 9 9900X, Apple M1/M4, Raspberry Pi 5), but none for 0.0.17.
corrections.compiler_and_flags: Clang is required: CMakeLists.txt aborts unless CMAKE_C_COMPILER_ID is Clang, and Windows uses clang-cl. CMake defaults to Release (-fomit-frame-pointer, -fno-stack-protector; LTO/PGO optional). PyPI wheels are built by a Nix flake in .github/workflows/release.yml. The Clang version is not stated anywhere, and the benchmark reports record only the CPython build compiler.
corrections.workload: dumps / dumps_to_bytes / loads (str and bytes input) on twitter.json, github.json, canada.json, mesh.json and simple_object_zh.json (README charts, v0.0.17). Measured with the companion ssrjson-benchmark package (src/ssrjson_benchmark/benchmark.py): the stdlib json baseline uses separators=(',', ':'), libraries are interleaved across rounds, and the process is pinned to one core. Python 3.14, x86-64 AVX2, compared against json, ujson, pydantic_core, msgspec and orjson.
corrections.caveats: A 39-star beta project whose numbers are all first-party: the benchmark repo Nambers/ssrJSON-benchmark (0 stars) is maintained by an ssrJSON contributor. Per-case figures appear only as labels inside the SVG charts. Neither the CPU behind the README charts nor the Clang version is stated. The baseline is CPython's stdlib json, which is not a named baseline for this category (baseline_in_list=false). Both ssrJSON and orjson use a global short-key cache in loads, which the benchmark README warns may not reflect production. dumps_to_bytes results depend on the UTF-8 cache setting. Requires x86-64-v2 (SSE4.2) or aarch64, and CPython only.

notes: The claims match the README text; I extracted the chart ratios from the SVG text labels. Metadata checks out: MIT, 39 stars, last commit 2026-09-17, not a fork. The per-CPU PDF reports in Nambers/ssrJSON-benchmark still omit the ssrJSON compiler version, so they do not lift the tier.
